name: Curl noise

contributors.name: Robert Bridson
contributors.detail: Coauthored Curl-Noise for Procedural Fluid Flow, constructing incompressible procedural velocity fields with controllable boundaries.
contributors.source: Bridson, Hourihan & Nordenstam, SIGGRAPH 2007 (author-hosted paper)

contributors.name: Jim Hourihan
contributors.detail: Coauthored the 2007 curl-noise method for procedural fluid-like motion.
contributors.source: Bridson, Hourihan & Nordenstam, SIGGRAPH 2007 (author-hosted paper)

contributors.name: Marcus Nordenstam
contributors.detail: Coauthored the 2007 curl-noise method, including treatment of solid boundaries.
contributors.source: Bridson, Hourihan & Nordenstam, SIGGRAPH 2007 (author-hosted paper)

caveat: The 2007 authors explicitly credit Kniss and Hart (2004) for earlier curl-of-Perlin-noise flow; this is a selected contribution, not a claim that the 2007 team invented every ingredient. The sketch is illustrative, not a complete fluid solver.

name: Domain warping

contributors.name: Ken Perlin
contributors.detail: Developed procedural noise and demonstrated domain displacement as a texture-building operation.
contributors.source: NYU Media Research Lab · procedural textures

contributors.name: Iñigo Quilez
contributors.detail: Mathias Isaksen's first-person account explicitly credits Quilez's 2002 domain-warping article as an earlier explanation of the technique.
contributors.source: Mathias Isaksen, Domain warping: an interactive introduction (2022)

contributors.name: Mathias Isaksen
contributors.detail: His illustrated tutorial documents domain-warped artworks and shows how to repeatedly displace sample positions with noise.
contributors.source: Artist's own tutorial, 18 March 2022

caveat: Domain warping is a family of coordinate transformations, not one invention. These entries distinguish procedural-texture foundations from later explanations and artistic uses.

name: Vector fields from math

contributors.name: Josiah Willard Gibbs
contributors.detail: Developed vector analysis as a practical mathematical language; his 1881–1884 Yale notes are preserved by the Smithsonian.
contributors.source: Smithsonian Libraries, Elements of vector analysis

contributors.name: Oliver Heaviside
contributors.detail: The Smithsonian identifies Heaviside alongside Gibbs as a developer of practical vector analysis.
contributors.source: Smithsonian Libraries, Elements of vector analysis

contributors.name: Tyler Hobbs
contributors.detail: Explains tracing paths through direction fields and shows how he uses and varies them in his own artwork.
contributors.source: Tyler Hobbs · Flow Fields

contributors.name: Gene Kogan
contributors.detail: His work index describes Vertex rivers as dots over vector fields. The work page documents a generative sketch, shown at Big Screen Plaza in January 2012, and links to its OpenProcessing code.
contributors.source: Artist’s work index · Vertex rivers

caveat: This is a broad mathematical family, not a named algorithm with one inventor; these are foundations of the language, not claims that Gibbs or Heaviside made this sketch or invented every vector-field technique.

name: Chladni / standing waves

contributors.name: Ernst Chladni
contributors.detail: Developed sand-covered vibrating-plate demonstrations that made nodal patterns visible.
contributors.source: Smithsonian, Chladni Plates

caveat: Chladni is credited for the experimental plate technique, not the whole theory of standing waves. Trigonometric sketches suggest nodal patterns but do not necessarily solve a physical plate's boundary-value problem.

name: Reaction–diffusion (Gray–Scott)

contributors.name: Alan Turing
contributors.detail: Proposed reaction and diffusion as a mechanism for the emergence of biological pattern.
contributors.source: Arizona State University, Embryo Project Encyclopedia

contributors.name: Peter Gray
contributors.detail: Coauthored the analysis of cubic autocatalysis and catalyst decay in an isothermal stirred reactor underlying the Gray–Scott model.
contributors.source: Gray & Scott, Chemical Engineering Science 39 (1984), 1087–1097; metadata verified through NII and CNRS records

contributors.name: Stephen K. Scott
contributors.detail: Coauthored the reaction-system analysis that supplies the named Gray–Scott chemical model.
contributors.source: Gray & Scott, Chemical Engineering Science 39 (1984), 1087–1097; metadata verified through NII and CNRS records

contributors.name: John E. Pearson
contributors.detail: His simulations demonstrated diverse irregular patterns and dividing spots in a simple reaction–diffusion system.
contributors.source: Pearson, Complex Patterns in a Simple System (1993), author preprint

contributors.name: Karl Sims
contributors.detail: His tutorial explains an implementation of Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion and ways of controlling the resulting patterns.
contributors.source: Karl Sims, Reaction-Diffusion Tutorial

caveat: Turing supplied a broader theoretical foundation, Gray and Scott the named chemistry, Pearson a major spatial-pattern study, and Sims a later tutorial. These roles are distinct; the illustrative sketch should not be presented as a validated numerical simulation.

name: Differential growth

contributors.name: Haiyi Liang
contributors.detail: Coauthored experiments and a thin-shell model showing how excess edge growth can drive a lily's blooming.
contributors.source: Liang & Mahadevan, PNAS (2011)

contributors.name: L. Mahadevan
contributors.detail: Coauthored the lily-growth study explicitly identified by Nervous System as an inspiration for Floraform.
contributors.source: Liang & Mahadevan, PNAS (2011); Floraform project credits

contributors.name: Jessica Rosenkrantz
contributors.detail: As a Nervous System cofounder, developed a studio practice whose Floraform system turns differential surface growth into sculptures and jewelry.
contributors.source: Nervous System, Floraform; studio authorship verified on About Us

contributors.name: Jesse Louis-Rosenberg
contributors.detail: As a Nervous System cofounder, developed a studio practice whose Floraform system simulates differently growing elastic surfaces.
contributors.source: Nervous System, Floraform; studio authorship verified on About Us

contributors.name: Anders Hoff
contributors.detail: His Differential Line code grows connected nodes and explicitly compares its behavior with Nervous System's Floraform.
contributors.source: Artist's own code; identity verified on inconvergent.net

caveat: Differential growth is a biological and mathematical family with no single inventor. These are a documented scientific study, a later design system, and a line-based artistic implementation; they are not interchangeable algorithms.

name: Diffusion-limited aggregation (DLA)

contributors.name: Thomas A. Witten Jr.
contributors.detail: Coauthored the original diffusion-limited aggregation paper studying random aggregates by computer simulation.
contributors.source: Witten & Sander, Physical Review Letters 47 (1981), 1400

contributors.name: Leonard M. Sander
contributors.detail: Coauthored the diffusion-limited aggregation model and its analysis of scaling in random aggregates.
contributors.source: Witten & Sander, Physical Review Letters 47 (1981), 1400

caveat: The original model has many later lattice, off-lattice, and artistic variants. A branching illustration alone does not establish that a sketch actually performs random-walk aggregation.

name: Space colonization

contributors.name: Adam Runions
contributors.detail: Coauthored the space-colonization tree model extending an earlier open leaf-venation model into three dimensions.
contributors.source: Runions, Lane & Prusinkiewicz, Eurographics Workshop on Natural Phenomena (2007)

contributors.name: Brendan Lane
contributors.detail: Coauthored the tree-growth algorithm whose parameters control visually relevant characteristics of tree shape.
contributors.source: Runions, Lane & Prusinkiewicz, Eurographics Workshop on Natural Phenomena (2007)

contributors.name: Przemysław Prusinkiewicz
contributors.detail: Coauthored the space-colonization model of trees based on geometric competition for available space.
contributors.source: Runions, Lane & Prusinkiewicz, Eurographics Workshop on Natural Phenomena (2007)

caveat: Credit here is for the named 2007 tree algorithm, not every model of plant growth; it builds on earlier leaf-venation work. The sketch is an illustration, not a claim to reproduce the full published method.

name: Physarum / slime mold

contributors.name: Jeff Jones
contributors.detail: Published a Physarum-inspired model in which simple chemotactic particles form and reorganize transport networks.
contributors.source: Jones, Artificial Life 16 (2010), 127–153; UWE institutional repository

caveat: Physarum research includes living-organism experiments and many mathematical models. Jones is credited for a particular influential agent model, not for discovering slime mold or inventing all slime-mold simulations; the sketch is illustrative.

name: Cellular automata beyond Life

contributors.name: Stephen Wolfram
contributors.detail: Analyzed self-organization and pattern formation in one-dimensional binary cellular automata.
contributors.source: Wolfram, Reviews of Modern Physics 55 (1983), 601

contributors.name: Bert Wang-Chak Chan
contributors.detail: Introduced Lenia, a cellular-automaton system with continuous space-time-state and a generalized local rule.
contributors.source: Chan, Lenia—Biology of Artificial Life (2018 preprint; 2019 publication)

caveat: This broad family has many contributors and no single inventor represented by this selection. Wolfram's elementary automata and Chan's Lenia are distinct examples beyond Life; neither is claimed to be the exact rule of the illustrative sketch.

name: Truchet tiles

contributors.name: Sébastien Truchet
contributors.detail: Studied combinations of square tiles divided diagonally into contrasting triangles in Mémoire sur les combinaisons.
contributors.source: Heidelberg Laureate Forum Foundation, Truchet Tilings

contributors.name: Cyril Stanley Smith
contributors.detail: Revisited Truchet's work in Leonardo and discussed alternative motifs including paired quarter-circle arcs.
contributors.source: Heidelberg Laureate Forum Foundation, Truchet Tilings

contributors.name: Pauline Boucher
contributors.detail: Translated Truchet's original text for the Leonardo publication that brought it to a later audience.
contributors.source: Heidelberg Laureate Forum Foundation, Truchet Tilings

caveat: Truchet's original motif is a divided square; the familiar arc motif belongs to later development. Smith is not asserted to be the first person ever to use quarter-circle tiles, and Boucher's contribution is translation.

name: Wang tiles

contributors.name: Hao Wang
contributors.detail: Introduced the combinatorial tile problem in Proving Theorems by Pattern Recognition—II.
contributors.source: Wang, Bell System Technical Journal 40 (1961), 1–41

contributors.name: Michael F. Cohen
contributors.detail: Coauthored a stochastic Wang-tile method for efficiently constructing nonperiodic textures, patterns, and geometry.
contributors.source: Cohen, Shade, Hiller & Deussen, ACM TOG (2003); author-hosted institutional page

contributors.name: Jonathan Shade
contributors.detail: Coauthored the Wang-tile graphics method for continuous nonperiodic image and texture generation.
contributors.source: Cohen, Shade, Hiller & Deussen, ACM TOG (2003); author-hosted institutional page

contributors.name: Stefan Hiller
contributors.detail: Coauthored the stochastic tiling and tile-filling methods presented in the 2003 graphics paper.
contributors.source: Cohen, Shade, Hiller & Deussen, ACM TOG (2003); author-hosted institutional page

contributors.name: Oliver Deussen
contributors.detail: Coauthored the graphics method applying edge-coded tiles to textures, sample distributions, and geometry.
contributors.source: Cohen, Shade, Hiller & Deussen, ACM TOG (2003); author-hosted institutional page

caveat: Wang's logical tiling system and its later graphics applications are different contributions. Not every matching tile set is aperiodic; an illustrative sketch need not solve the infinite-plane tiling problem.

name: Wallpaper groups

contributors.name: Evgraf S. Fedorov
contributors.detail: The IUCr history credits Fedorov with the first description of the 17 plane symmetry groups in 1890 or 1891.
contributors.source: International Union of Crystallography, Appeal of Symmetry (2025)

contributors.name: George Pólya
contributors.detail: Enumerated the 17 plane symmetry groups and illustrated each with a tiling, helping connect the mathematics to decorative art.
contributors.source: International Union of Crystallography, Appeal of Symmetry (2025)

contributors.name: M. C. Escher
contributors.detail: Studied Pólya's diagrams and used a tiling derived from that study in Development I.
contributors.source: International Union of Crystallography, Appeal of Symmetry (2025)

caveat: These people contributed to classification, exposition, and later art; they did not invent the long cultural history of repeating ornament. A sketch that repeats motifs may show only one group rather than all 17.

name: Girih / Islamic star patterns

contributors.name: Peter J. Lu
contributors.detail: Coauthored a study interpreting medieval girih designs through decorated polygonal tiles and self-similar transformations.
contributors.source: Author research page and Science paper

contributors.name: Paul J. Steinhardt
contributors.detail: Coauthored the study of decagonal and nearly quasicrystalline order in medieval Islamic architectural patterns.
contributors.source: Author research page and Science paper

contributors.name: Gülru Necipoğlu
contributors.detail: Authored The Topkapı Scroll, a historical study of geometry and ornament in Islamic architecture.
contributors.source: Getty, The Topkapı Scroll (1995)

contributors.name: Mohammad al-Asad
contributors.detail: Contributed the essay on the geometry of muqarnas to The Topkapı Scroll.
contributors.source: Getty, The Topkapı Scroll (1995)

caveat: Islamic geometric ornament is a centuries-long, collective artistic tradition with no single inventor; these named scholars are interpreters, not the original artisans. The quasicrystalline reading concerns particular examples, not all girih, and al-Asad’s documented contribution concerns adjacent muqarnas geometry.

name: Penrose / aperiodic

contributors.name: Roger Penrose
contributors.detail: Developed the aperiodic tilings bearing his name and described his construction in 1974.
contributors.source: AMS Notices, September 2023

contributors.name: Robert Berger
contributors.detail: Authored the 1966 proof that the general domino tiling problem is undecidable.
contributors.source: AMS publisher notice for Memoir 66

caveat: Penrose tilings are one specific family within aperiodic tiling theory; Berger is credited for earlier foundations, not for Penrose’s tiles. A finite decorative patch alone does not prove aperiodicity.

name: Hyperbolic tilings {p,q}

contributors.name: H. S. M. Coxeter
contributors.detail: Sent Escher a symmetry paper whose hyperbolic tiling diagram helped inspire the Circle Limit series.
contributors.source: AMS, How Did Escher Do It?

contributors.name: M. C. Escher
contributors.detail: Studied Coxeter’s diagram and translated hyperbolic repetition into his Circle Limit woodcuts.
contributors.source: AMS, How Did Escher Do It?

contributors.name: Henri Poincaré
contributors.detail: The AMS account describes the unit-disk model of hyperbolic geometry as attributed to Poincaré.
contributors.source: AMS, How Did Escher Do It?

caveat: Hyperbolic geometry and regular tilings have a broad mathematical history; this selection traces a model and an artistic exchange, not a single invention. Escher’s motif boundaries need not all be hyperbolic geodesics.

name: L-systems

contributors.name: Aristid Lindenmayer
contributors.detail: Developed formal growth models for cellular interactions, including branching filaments.
contributors.source: Lindenmayer, Journal of Theoretical Biology (1968), institutional copy

contributors.name: Przemysław Prusinkiewicz
contributors.detail: Presented turtle interpretation of L-system strings to generate fractal curves and plant-like pictures.
contributors.source: Author publication page, Graphics Interface 1986

caveat: The biological rewriting formalism and its graphical interpretation are distinct contributions; many later extensions and collaborators are outside this short selection.

name: Recursive subdivision

contributors.name: Edwin Catmull
contributors.detail: Coauthored a recursive method producing B-spline surfaces on meshes of arbitrary topology.
contributors.source: Catmull and Clark, Computer-Aided Design (1978), Berkeley-hosted original

contributors.name: James Clark
contributors.detail: Coauthored the generalization of recursive bicubic B-spline subdivision to arbitrary mesh topology.
contributors.source: Catmull and Clark, Computer-Aided Design (1978), Berkeley-hosted original

caveat: Recursive subdivision is a general strategy with no single inventor. Catmull and Clark are a documented graphics branch; splitting a flat canvas into rectangles is not automatically Catmull–Clark surface subdivision.

name: Chaos game / IFS

contributors.name: John E. Hutchinson
contributors.detail: Developed a rigorous theory of self-similar sets and measures generated by finite families of contractions.
contributors.source: Hutchinson, Fractals and Self Similarity (1981), author copy

contributors.name: Michael Barnsley
contributors.detail: Coauthored a theorem showing when a chaos-game orbit yields an attractor for a general iterated function system.
contributors.source: Barnsley and Vince, The Chaos Game on a General Iterated Function System

contributors.name: Andrew Vince
contributors.detail: Coauthored the general chaos-game theorem, including settings beyond contractive IFS.
contributors.source: Barnsley and Vince, The Chaos Game on a General Iterated Function System

caveat: This links foundational IFS theory with later random-iteration research; it does not assign sole invention of every chaos-game variant to these authors.

name: Fractal fracture

contributors.name: Alain Fournier
contributors.detail: Coauthored recursive stochastic subdivision methods for rendering rough curves and surfaces.
contributors.source: Fournier, Fussell & Carpenter · Computer Rendering of Stochastic Models (1982)

contributors.name: Donald Fussell
contributors.detail: Coauthored recursive stochastic subdivision methods for rendering rough curves and surfaces.
contributors.source: Fournier, Fussell & Carpenter · Computer Rendering of Stochastic Models (1982)

contributors.name: Loren Carpenter
contributors.detail: Coauthored recursive stochastic subdivision methods for rendering rough curves and surfaces.
contributors.source: Fournier, Fussell & Carpenter · Computer Rendering of Stochastic Models (1982)

caveat: The catalog’s rough-edge sketch is closest to recursive random displacement. These authors document that graphics lineage; this is not a claim that the sketch simulates physical fracture.

name: Strange attractors

contributors.name: Edward N. Lorenz
contributors.detail: Demonstrated unstable nonperiodic trajectories in a simplified deterministic convection model.
contributors.source: Lorenz, Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow (1963)

contributors.name: David Ruelle
contributors.detail: Coauthored a proposed mechanism for turbulence in dissipative systems using strange attractors.
contributors.source: Ruelle and Takens, On the Nature of Turbulence (1971)

contributors.name: Floris Takens
contributors.detail: Coauthored the mathematical turbulence proposal describing strange attractors.
contributors.source: Ruelle and Takens, On the Nature of Turbulence (1971)

caveat: Strange attractors are a family of dynamical objects, not one curve or one formula; a visually tangled trajectory alone does not demonstrate chaos.

name: Harmonographs / Lissajous

contributors.name: Jules Lissajous
contributors.detail: Developed an optical method for studying vibrations associated with the curves named after him.
contributors.source: Science Museum Group, Sympalmograph collection record

contributors.name: John Browning
contributors.detail: Made the circa-1877 sympalmograph, a harmonograph variant drawing combined perpendicular harmonic motions.
contributors.source: Science Museum Group, Sympalmograph collection record

contributors.name: Zach Lieberman
contributors.detail: Authored the openFrameworks animation chapter, including a Lissajous section demonstrating different angular rates for horizontal and vertical motion. A contemporary teaching contribution; Jules Antoine Lissajous remains credited for the historical curves.
contributors.source: ofBook · animation chapter by Zach Lieberman

caveat: Harmonographs are a family of instruments with no single inventor established here; Lissajous’s optical work and Browning’s manufactured drawing machine are different contributions.

name: Double pendulum / N-body trails

contributors.name: Troy Shinbrot
contributors.detail: Coauthored an experimental and numerical demonstration of sensitive dependence in a double pendulum.
contributors.source: Shinbrot, Grebogi, Wisdom and Yorke, American Journal of Physics (1992)

contributors.name: Celso Grebogi
contributors.detail: Coauthored the double-pendulum study measuring exponential growth of initially small separations.
contributors.source: Shinbrot, Grebogi, Wisdom and Yorke, American Journal of Physics (1992)

contributors.name: Jack Wisdom
contributors.detail: Coauthored the comparison between measured double-pendulum motion and numerical simulations.
contributors.source: Shinbrot, Grebogi, Wisdom and Yorke, American Journal of Physics (1992)

contributors.name: James A. Yorke
contributors.detail: Coauthored the laboratory demonstration of chaotic double-pendulum motion.
contributors.source: Shinbrot, Grebogi, Wisdom and Yorke, American Journal of Physics (1992)

contributors.name: Josh Barnes
contributors.detail: Coauthored a hierarchical tree algorithm for efficiently calculating gravitational forces among many bodies.
contributors.source: Barnes and Hut, Nature (1986)

contributors.name: Piet Hut
contributors.detail: Coauthored the recursive spatial-subdivision method now called the Barnes–Hut algorithm.
contributors.source: Barnes and Hut, Nature (1986)

caveat: These are two different mechanics recipes grouped by their visible trails. The cited researchers did not invent pendulums, gravity, or all N-body methods; a small direct-sum simulation need not use Barnes–Hut.

name: Orbit traps

contributors.name: Clifford A. Pickover
contributors.detail: Developed the epsilon-cross method identified by Carlson as a precursor to his 3-D stalk rendering.
contributors.source: Carlson, Computers & Graphics (1999), introduction

contributors.name: Paul W. Carlson
contributors.detail: Presented two artistic orbit-trap rendering methods for Newton M-set fractals and described extensions of Pickover’s approach.
contributors.source: Carlson, Computers & Graphics (1999)

caveat: Orbit traps color an iterated orbit using its relationship to a geometric target; they are a rendering family distinct from the underlying fractal formula.

name: Poisson-disk / blue noise

contributors.name: Robert L. Cook
contributors.detail: Showed how appropriately nonuniform sampling turns structured aliasing into less objectionable noise.
contributors.source: Cook, Stochastic Sampling in Computer Graphics (1986), Pixar archive

contributors.name: Robert Bridson
contributors.detail: Presented a linear-time Poisson-disk sampler using an active list, local candidates and a background grid.
contributors.source: Bridson, ACM SIGGRAPH 2007 Sketches

caveat: Blue noise describes spectral behavior, while Poisson-disk sampling imposes minimum spacing; the terms are related but not interchangeable, and neither broad tradition has one inventor.

name: Dithering as art

contributors.name: Robert W. Floyd
contributors.detail: Coauthored An Adaptive Algorithm for Spatial Greyscale, the paper associated with Floyd–Steinberg dithering.
contributors.source: University of Magdeburg bibliography for Floyd and Steinberg (1976)

contributors.name: Louis Steinberg
contributors.detail: Coauthored the spatial-greyscale algorithm jointly credited as Floyd–Steinberg dithering.
contributors.source: University of Magdeburg bibliography for Floyd and Steinberg (1976)

contributors.name: Donald E. Knuth
contributors.detail: Published Digital Halftones by Dot Diffusion, another documented route from continuous tones to discrete marks.
contributors.source: Stanford profile publication record

contributors.name: Golan Levin
contributors.role: Teaching · Code as Creative Medium co-author
contributors.detail: Co-authored the creative-coding book and its shared example collection, including this random-dot dithering exercise. The repository credits assistance from Lingdong Huang, Tatyana Mustakos, Cassie Scheirer, and Xinyi (Joyce) Wang. This is a teaching credit, not sole implementation or invention.
contributors.source: Code as Creative Medium · example and repository credits

contributors.name: Tega Brain
contributors.role: Teaching · Code as Creative Medium co-author
contributors.detail: Co-authored the creative-coding book and its shared example collection, including this random-dot dithering exercise. The repository credits assistance from Lingdong Huang, Tatyana Mustakos, Cassie Scheirer, and Xinyi (Joyce) Wang. This is a teaching credit, not sole implementation or invention.
contributors.source: Code as Creative Medium · example and repository credits

caveat: Dithering as an artistic practice has no single inventor. These are named technical contributors to halftoning methods, not a claim that they originated every artistic use or ordered-dither pattern.

name: Halftone systems

contributors.name: Robert W. Floyd
contributors.detail: Coauthored the 1976 spatial-greyscale paper underlying Floyd–Steinberg error diffusion.
contributors.source: University of Magdeburg: Floyd and Steinberg (1976)

contributors.name: Louis Steinberg
contributors.detail: Coauthored An Adaptive Algorithm for Spatial Greyscale with Robert Floyd.
contributors.source: Japan Science and Technology Agency: 1976 publication record

contributors.name: Bryce E. Bayer
contributors.detail: Authored the 1973 paper An Optimum Method for Two-Level Rendition of Continuous-Tone Pictures.
contributors.source: National Diet Library: Bayer (1973)

caveat: Halftoning is a broad printing and imaging tradition; these are selected digital methods, not a single invention.

name: TSP art / scribble fill

contributors.name: Robert Bosch
contributors.detail: Developed continuous-line TSP drawings with Adrianne Herman, then coauthored the 2005 improvements with Craig Kaplan.
contributors.source: Kaplan and Bosch: TSP Art (2005)

contributors.name: Adrianne Herman
contributors.detail: Coauthored Continuous Line Drawings via the Traveling Salesman Problem with Robert Bosch in 2004.
contributors.source: University of Waterloo: TSP Art Instances

contributors.name: Craig S. Kaplan
contributors.detail: Coauthored TSP Art, introducing improved city distributions based on stippling and ordered dithering.
contributors.source: Kaplan and Bosch: TSP Art (2005)

caveat: This attribution covers the TSP branch; free scribble fills are a broader family with different methods.

name: Weighted Voronoi stippling

contributors.name: Adrian Secord
contributors.detail: Presented image-based stippling using weighted centroidal Voronoi diagrams in 2002.
contributors.source: Secord: Weighted Voronoi Stippling (2002)

caveat: Secord's specific image-stippling method builds on earlier Voronoi and centroidal-relaxation mathematics.

name: Circle packing, grown

contributors.name: Daniel Shiffman
contributors.detail: Demonstrated growing circles with boundary and overlap tests in Coding Challenge 50.
contributors.source: The Coding Train: Circle Packing

contributors.name: Marius Watz
contributors.detail: Shiffman's grown-circle tutorial explicitly introduces Watz's circle-packing work as a reference.
contributors.source: The Coding Train: Circle Packing, introductory credit

caveat: These are documented creative-coding influences, not inventors of the much older mathematical circle-packing problem.

name: Voronoi/Delaunay operated on

contributors.name: Georgy Voronoy
contributors.detail: Studied the tessellations now known as Voronoi diagrams in his geometry-of-numbers work.
contributors.source: University of St Andrews: Georgy Voronoy

contributors.name: Boris Delaunay
contributors.detail: Authored the 1934 empty-sphere paper Sur la sphère vide, dedicated to Georges Voronoï.
contributors.source: Math-Net: Delaunay (1934)

caveat: These names identify mathematical foundations; artistic edge, cell, and mesh operations have no single originator.

name: Minimum spanning tree / relative neighborhood graphs

contributors.name: Joseph B. Kruskal
contributors.detail: Published On the Shortest Spanning Subtree of a Graph and the Traveling Salesman Problem in 1956.
contributors.source: CiNii / AMS: Kruskal (1956)

contributors.name: Godfried T. Toussaint
contributors.detail: Defined the relative neighbourhood graph and proved its relationship to the MST and Delaunay triangulation in 1980.
contributors.source: Toussaint: The Relative Neighbourhood Graph of a Finite Planar Set (1980)

caveat: MST algorithms have several independent historical contributors; these are selected foundations, not an exhaustive credit list.

name: Hidden-line 3D → 2D

contributors.name: Lawrence G. Roberts
contributors.detail: His 1963 MIT thesis describes removing back lines and line segments obscured by other objects.
contributors.source: MIT: Machine Perception of Three-Dimensional Solids (1963)

caveat: Roberts is an early documented contributor; later hidden-line and hidden-surface algorithms form a large research field.

name: Superformula / supershapes

contributors.name: Johan Gielis
contributors.detail: Introduced the Superformula as a single parametric equation for many natural and abstract shapes in 2003.
contributors.source: Gielis: American Journal of Botany (2003)

contributors.name: Paul Bourke
contributors.detail: Published 3D supershape examples and software based on Gielis's equations and a spherical product.
contributors.source: Paul Bourke: Supershapes (July 2003)

caveat: Gielis authored the formula; Bourke is credited here for the documented 3D exposition, not for inventing the formula.

name: Moiré

contributors.name: Carlos Cruz-Diez
contributors.detail: His 1964 Chromointerférence arose from sliding one repeated-line image over another transparent line pattern.
contributors.source: Cruz-Diez official archive: Chromointerférence (1964)

contributors.name: Golan Levin
contributors.role: Teaching · Code as Creative Medium co-author
contributors.detail: Co-authored the creative-coding book and its shared example collection, including this moiré exercise. The repository credits assistance from Lingdong Huang, Tatyana Mustakos, Cassie Scheirer, and Xinyi (Joyce) Wang. This is a teaching credit, not sole implementation or invention.
contributors.source: Code as Creative Medium · example and repository credits

contributors.name: Tega Brain
contributors.role: Teaching · Code as Creative Medium co-author
contributors.detail: Co-authored the creative-coding book and its shared example collection, including this moiré exercise. The repository credits assistance from Lingdong Huang, Tatyana Mustakos, Cassie Scheirer, and Xinyi (Joyce) Wang. This is a teaching credit, not sole implementation or invention.
contributors.source: Code as Creative Medium · example and repository credits

contributors.name: Gene Kogan
contributors.detail: Used repeated deltoid curves to produce moiré patterns in Interference. His account says the original code was lost; the work documents an artistic application, not invention of moiré.
contributors.source: Artist’s work record · Interference

caveat: Moiré is an optical phenomenon with a long history; Cruz-Diez is a documented artistic example, not its inventor.

name: Wave interference

contributors.name: Thomas Young
contributors.detail: Explained light interference through the superposition of waves in his early-nineteenth-century work.
contributors.source: Institute of Physics: Superposition

caveat: A physical principle used by many visual recipes; Young's role is foundational physics, not authorship of a modern art algorithm.

name: Metaballs / implicit fields

contributors.name: Jim Blinn
contributors.detail: His 1982 paper renders surfaces formed by summed Gaussian density distributions.
contributors.source: Microsoft Research: A Generalization of Algebraic Surface Drawing

contributors.name: Paul Bourke
contributors.detail: Explains implicit-surface blending under the names metaballs, blobbies, and soft objects.
contributors.source: Paul Bourke: Implicit Surfaces

caveat: Implicit surfaces predate metaball modeling; this is a selected lineage rather than a complete history of soft-object research.

name: fBm + ridged / turbulent

contributors.name: Benoît Mandelbrot
contributors.detail: Coauthored the 1968 study Fractional Brownian Motions, Fractional Noises and Applications.
contributors.source: Mandelbrot and Van Ness: SIAM Review (1968)

contributors.name: John W. Van Ness
contributors.detail: Coauthored the 1968 paper formalizing and studying fractional Brownian motions.
contributors.source: Mandelbrot and Van Ness: SIAM Review (1968)

contributors.name: Ken Perlin
contributors.detail: Introduced a procedural noise-based image synthesizer including synthetic turbulence in 1985.
contributors.source: Perlin: An Image Synthesizer (1985)

contributors.name: F. Kenton Musgrave
contributors.detail: Developed ridged multifractal noise used for mountainous terrain, as credited in LightWave's texture documentation.
contributors.source: LightWave 2025 documentation: Ridged Multifractal

contributors.name: Craig E. Kolb
contributors.detail: Coauthored the 1989 paper on fractal terrain noise synthesis, erosion, and rendering.
contributors.source: Musgrave, Kolb and Mace (1989)

contributors.name: Robert S. Mace
contributors.detail: Coauthored the 1989 paper on fractal terrain noise synthesis, erosion, and rendering.
contributors.source: Musgrave, Kolb and Mace (1989)

contributors.name: Lauren Lee McCarthy
contributors.detail: Created p5.js, whose noiseDetail API exposes octave and falloff controls for layered Perlin noise. This credits the enabling platform, not invention of fBm, implementation of every noise function, or all ridged/turbulent variants.
contributors.source: p5.js · octave and falloff documentation

caveat: Graphics 'fBm' usually means a finite noise-octave construction, not exact stochastic fBm; ridged and turbulent variants also have distinct histories.

name: SDF raymarching

contributors.name: John C. Hart
contributors.detail: His 1996 sphere-tracing paper advances rays using geometric distance bounds that avoid crossing the surface.
contributors.source: University of Illinois: Sphere Tracing (1996)

contributors.name: Iñigo Quilez
contributors.detail: Presented distance-field rendering techniques in Rendering Worlds with Two Triangles.
contributors.source: Iñigo Quilez: Rendering Worlds with Two Triangles (2008)

caveat: Sphere tracing is a distance-guided form of raymarching; it should not be conflated with every fixed-step volume raymarcher.

name: Feedback buffers

contributors.name: James P. Crutchfield
contributors.detail: Modeled video-feedback dynamics and reproduced their behavior with digital simulations in 1984.
contributors.source: Crutchfield: Space-Time Dynamics in Video Feedback (1984)

contributors.name: Steina Vasulka
contributors.detail: Described her early video-feedback experiments in a preserved 1997 interview.
contributors.source: Vasulka Interviews: Steina on video feedback (1997)

contributors.name: Woody Vasulka
contributors.detail: Discussed analog feedback loops and feedback in digital devices in a preserved 1996 interview.
contributors.source: Vasulka Interviews: Woody on feedback (1996)

contributors.name: Olivia Jack
contributors.detail: Created Hydra, a live-coding video-synthesis environment with feedback influences documented in its source repository.
contributors.source: Hydra: official repository and contributor credits

caveat: Digital frame-buffer feedback is a broad technique; analog-video precedents and later software tools are distinct contributions.
